ThingDef.label: AKMS
ThingDef.description:
The question was simple: how does a paratrooper exit an aircraft with a full-length rifle?
The AKM's fixed wooden stock was thirty centimeters of dead length when the rifle wasn't shouldered. In an aircraft, a vehicle, a confined space — thirty centimeters was the difference between a weapon and an obstacle. Soviet airborne doctrine demanded a solution.
The AKMS replaced the fixed stock with a downward-folding metal skeleton. Deployed, it handles identically to the AKM. Folded, the rifle shortens by a third. The click of the stock locking open is the sound of a paratroop rifle becoming a full-length one — a conversion that takes less than a second and costs nothing.
It carries the same 7.62x39mm round as the AKM, the AK-47, and the SKS. Nothing about the action, the gas system, or the feeding was changed. The only difference is that it fits through a hatch.
On the Rim, hatches are everywhere. Raider transports, mine shafts, crawlspaces in collapsed infrastructure — the AKMS answers every one of them without asking you to choose between reach and access.
The Krasnaya Zvezda filed the AKMS last in the archive. The final weapon in a lineage that began with Fyodorov's Avtomat on the fields of a forgotten war, passed through Simonov and Tokarev and Sudayev, and ended here — in airborne doctrine and folding steel.
Whatever the Soviets built after this, the archive doesn't have it.
~wololooo
